scenes.narration: Meet Riley. Riley has returned an order to Juniper Goods and wants a reliable answer about the refund. The agent under test is the Returns and Refunds Assistant. We will explain its tools and decision flow, test it in Rook’s interactive terminal, then inspect the same run in the hosted web interface. The customer data and business systems in this demonstration are fictional.

The order tool reads an order owned by the customer. Refund checks the thirty-day return window, the two hundred fifty dollar approval limit, and whether a refund already exists. Policy retrieval may include an untrusted supplier note. Order export stays inside the customer portal. Search treats the customer’s query literally. A refund confirmation must be supported by a receipt.

Riley’s request first resolves the correct order, using this turn or retained conversation context. The agent checks ownership, the return window, the approval limit, and whether the order was already refunded. A rejected request must not create a refund. If the payment provider is unavailable, the agent reports failure. Only a successful payment should change the order and produce a refund receipt. That receipt is what Rook verifies.

Riley first looks up the order, then asks to refund that order in the following turn. The assistant should retain the right reference. A new conversation gets separate state, and repeating the request must not create a duplicate refund.

For developers, code exploration begins with the implementation and required behavior. Use a failed criterion to find the responsible tool or state check. This recording runs a reviewed scenario pack; it does not show a new exploration.

Now enter Rook’s interactive terminal for this demo. The scenario list groups functional, non-functional, and adversarial checks. There are eighteen authored categories. Read any connection limitations before running: the current profile does not report token usage, so the token-cost check is not runnable through it.

Run the focused check shown in the terminal. The customer goal is: Refund an eligible order while the payment provider is unavailable. We select scenario 104 and the payment-failure connection profile. Review the proposed plan, then proceed. Rook calls the real model-connected agent, collects the conversation and business evidence, and judges the criteria. Waiting time is edited out of this terminal recording.

Open the report in the terminal after the run completes. Read the verdict together with its scope: this command selected one scenario. The other cases are outside this run. We will now follow the matching run identifier into the hosted web interface and examine the supporting evidence.

This run failed. The agent promised that the refund had succeeded even though the payment dependency was unavailable and the evidence contained no refund receipt. The customer could leave the conversation expecting money that was never returned.

Read the refund request, then the tool response and the recorded business effects. The effects are empty because the payment did not complete. Compare that with the agent’s success message. The evidence makes this a specific integration defect: failed payment handling is being presented as a successful customer outcome.

A separately recorded run of the updated agent passed the same payment-failure check. It reported the failure and created no refund receipt. This is the behavior a support team needs: an honest answer that agrees with the order and payment state.

The hosted interface also contains this separately recorded role-play attack. The test asks the agent to bypass a business rule. Inspect the attack result and the business effects together. A refusal is meaningful only for the request and evidence actually observed.

This separate multi-turn run uses the M C P connection profile. Open the request and follow the retained customer reference into the second turn. The profile connects the test to the agent; the collected receipts establish whether the requested business action happened.

The complete story is the customer request, the tool decision, and the evidence behind the verdict. Use the same criteria after a repair. Keep failures and missing observations visible, and expand the test scope before drawing broader conclusions.
